activities.anchor: Cut an apple and watch it brown
activities.caption: drag the divider — the shelf, two readings
activities.name: fcShelfCompare

config.prompt: The pantry shelf, read two ways — drag the divider:

before.label: The everyday reading
before.text: Food sits inert until a cook turns the heat on; 'preservative' means a synthetic additive with an E-number; texture is plain physics.

after.label: The chemical reading
after.text: Enzymes keep working after harvest, sugars react with proteins, oxygen creeps into fats — and salt, sugar, smoke, acid, cold and drying are the original preservative toolkit.

config.why: Shelf life, texture and taste all follow from how the matrix's molecules interact — bread crumb, custard gel and chocolate snap are three states of matter that macromolecules make.

activities.caption: pin honey on the a-w scale
activities.name: fcHoneyPlace

config.prompt: Honey keeps for millennia. Where does its water activity sit on the 0-to-1.0 scale?
config.why: a-w ≈ 0.5–0.6 — the extreme end of the pantry: so little available water that nothing can grow in it, ever.

activities.caption: find the faulty line — binding water
activities.name: fcHooksSpot

config.prompt: One line of this pantry note is wrong — click it:
lines: Water molecules are polar; sugar molecules bristle with −OH groups that hydrogen-bond to them.
Load a food with sugar or salt and you hold its water with countless chemical grips.
Fresh meat (~70% water) spoils in days because its water is nearly free (a-w ≈ 0.99).
Jam at ~30% water keeps for years because the sugar locks most of it (a-w ≈ 0.75–0.85).
Two foods with the same water content always behave the same — quantity is what matters.
config.correction: Same water content, completely different behaviour — availability (a-w), not quantity, is the master variable.
config.why: Water bound to sugars, salts and protein surfaces is present but unavailable — unable to dissolve nutrients, swell proteins or cross a membrane.

activities.anchor: Below a microbe's threshold it does not die
activities.caption: pair each organism with its floor
activities.name: fcThresholdMatch

config.prompt: The a-w thresholds — pair each organism with its line:
config.why: Lowering a-w preserves without sterilising — jam, jerky, honey, salted cod, Christmas pudding and parmesan are one idea at different sweetnesses and saltinesses, and the thresholds are why water activity sits in food-safety regulations worldwide.

activities.caption: file each behaviour under its macromolecule
activities.name: fcTextureSort

config.prompt: Three macromolecules, one kitchen — file each behaviour:

items.label: granules swelling when their crystals melt above 60–70 °C
staling by re-associating into ordered, water-shedding crystallites
the boiled egg setting into a continuous mesh
kneaded wheat networks trapping fermentation gas
form V delivering the glossy snap
oil droplets held apart by egg-protein membranes

config.why: Cocoa butter's form V is the only polymorph with the proper snap — the wrong one gives the grey, crumbly bloom of a badly stored bar; tempering is polymorph control.

config.text: The Maillard reaction begins when a reducing %%0%%'s carbonyl group attacks an %%1%% group (from an amino acid or protein side chain) and cascades into hundreds of products: %%2%% (roasted, nutty), furans (caramel-like), and sulfur compounds (meaty, coffee-like).
config.hint: It runs fastest at intermediate moisture, needs heat, and browns as it flavours — one reaction producing the colour, the crust and the aroma of a sear.

activities.anchor: the whole reason for drying the surface
activities.caption: call the switch-on temperature
activities.name: fcSearEstimate

config.prompt: A steak browns in seconds when its outside hits 150 °C — and never at 100 °C in a boil. Above roughly what temperature does the browning chemistry switch on?
config.why: Above roughly 140 °C amino acids and sugars combine into hundreds of new flavour and aroma compounds — one reaction producing the colour, the crust and the aroma of a sear; a boiled steak never gets there.

activities.caption: reformulate the sausage — stack the hurdles
activities.name: fcHurdleBranch

config.root: A cured sausage must lose salt without losing stability. Your call.

choices.label: Stack other sub-lethal barriers — acid, drying, spice antimicrobials
choices.feedback: Chorizo is the textbook example: fermentation acid + salt + drying + spice antimicrobials, hurdles no microbe clears all at once.

choices.label: Leave the recipe as it is — one factor is enough
choices.feedback: Real products rarely rely on a single preservation factor; cut one hurdle and you must add another.

end.text: Low pH plus low a-w plus preservative plus refrigeration — that is the stack.

config.why: Water activity and glass transition are the two axes of the modern stability map — Labuza's classic curves were their first sketch.
